```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(survey)
```

A school wants to estimate the average score on a reading comprehension exam for sixth grade students. The school’s students are grouped into 3 tracks, based on their performance in reading classes in 5th grade. The school decides to stratify on tracks because this method should reduce the variability of test scores. The sixth grade contains a total of 55 students in track I, 80 in track II, and 65 in track III. A stratified random sample is taken with 14 students in track I, 20 students in track II, and 16 students in track III. 

The data for the **sample** of students are located in the file `10-sixthgrade.csv` file on canvas.

4.	Use the appropriate equations to *estimate* the average score for the sixth grade (i.e. calculate $\bar{y}_st$). Do all the calculations by hand, only rounding it at the end to 3 significant decimal places. Show your work!

5.	Now use the `survey` package in to calculate the standard error. Calculate the 95% confidence interval for the parameter of interest "by hand" using the mean and standard error and a critical value of 2. 

```{r}
readingdat <- readingdat |> 
  mutate(weight = SIZE / n(), .by = TRACK)

strat_des <- svydesign(ids = ~1,
                       strata = ~TRACK,
                       weights = ~ weight,
                       data = readingdat)

svymean(~SCORES, design = strat_des, na.rm = T)
```

## Sample Size

12. Suppose the *average test score* for the class is to be estimated *again at the end of the school year* with a bound of four points on the error of estimation. The costs of sampling are equal in all strata, but the variances differ. Assume the variances are in line with what we saw in the study at the beginning of the year. Find the overall sample size and the sample size for each stratum using the *appropriate allocation*. Do all the calculations by hand and show your work.

Make sure that you make clear what your:

- allocation method
- allocations ($a_g$'s)
- overall sample size $n$
- and stratum sample sizes ($n_g$'s) are.
